The simple object of this Bill *is to provide for the registration by the government of union labels. At the present time union labels are being used in this country by certain labour organizations, in agreement with the men who produce the article, and it has been found by experience that these labels are counterfeit. The object of this Bill is to provide for the registration of these labels and, to this extent, to protect union labour.

pose any gentleman in
this House were offered two mortgages- one a mortgage on a property, say for $12,000, taking first rank, and the other a mortgage for $4,000, coming second, which would correspond with the proportion existing between the government and tlie Grand Trunk mortgages. If the first mortgagee has his mortgage dated and registered first, everybody can see that it takes precedence, and that the other is entirely subject to it, just as last, year the Grand Trunk mortgage was subject to that of the government. But suppose in the mortgage, which was first in point of time and registration, there was a clause providing that no step whatever could be taken by the mortgagee to collect principle or interest for a hundred years, can there be any doubt that, in such a case, the second mortgage practically became the first ? Is there any one who would not prefer the second ? Suppose that the terms of years in which the first mortgagee could not take any proceedings were 50 instead of 100 or 15 years instead of 50, would not tlie first mortgage take practically the second place to a corresponding extent ? If the property were good for the $12,000, the amount of the first mortgage, and nothing more, the second mortgagee would undoubtedly, during the fifteen years in which the first mortgage was precluded from taking any action, take good care to collect his principle and interest before his predecessor could have any opportunity of cutting the ground from under him. Consequently, we find that although the Grand Trunk mortgage ranks second, the operation of the first is suspended for fifteen years, taking that and nothing more, the second mortgage practically becomes the first.
But that is not all. During the fifteen years the holders of the second mortgage have the exercise of all their rights. They can sue and distrain for interest, they can take all the remedies they are entitled to as mortgagees, while the first mortgagee is tied up. But even when the fifteen years come to an enfi and the first mortgagee is allowed to wake up from his Rip Van Winkle slumber, he cannot sue or foreclose. All he can do is, put a receiver in charge to operate the road and apply the surplus profits, after paying operating expenses, pari passu- heaven forgive us-between the two mortgagees, so that the so-called first mortgage becomes in no way superior to the second. If the receiver collect $100 net profits, $75 will go to the government and $25 to the Grand Trunk Railway. Both are in all respects on the same footing with regard to the moneys collected by the receiver Let me consider this further. During the fifteen years, during which nothing has been paid on the first mortgage, there was of course a tremendous increase of debt. Suppose the interest were only three per cent, three per cent in fifteen years on $100,000,000 would', 'give $45,000,000. So that in fifteen years, by simple interest alone, the amount due the first mortgagee would almost be fifty per cent above what it was originally, and his claim would be much greater. Whereas the second mortgagee would have either exactly the same claim as originally, because he would have collected the interest during the interval, or a lesser claim or possibly would have been paid in full. Therefore when the receiver steps in, the Grand Trunk Railway will have succeeded in having its liability reduced or wiped out altogether by getting its bonds paid in the interval and in any event it is on an equal footing with the government as regards the division of the net profits. Why is it, when the head of the firm asked for a change in the financial conditions, that the government, which has no pecuniary interests in the outcome of the road, should allow its position to be lowered to that of a second mortgagee, while the Grand Trunk Railway, which has so much to take out of the enterprise, should be given the position of first mortgagee ?
What is the Grand Trunk doing ? A great deal has been said of the desirability of carrying out the contract, because it is going to secure trade for Canadian ports. I know that this question of securing trade for Canadian ports, that this is a dangerous subject, for it is one on which one is apt to be misunderstood. Perhaps there was never a truer remark, or one more thoroughly misunderstood, than the famous remark of Dr. Johnson, that patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel. Although everybody knew that no more patriotic man ever lived than Dr. Johnson, those opposed to him chose to apply that remark in a different way altogether to that which he intended. The idea he intended to convey was that patriotism is so great a virtue, that a scoundrel, who had none in his composition, would try to cover up his rascalities by assuming the appearance of that virtue. In like manner there is a great assumption of virtue and a great deal of nonsense spoken about bringing traffic to Canadian ports, and many attempts are made to deceive the people in connection with that question. I am as anxious as any one to see the traffic of the country carried through Canadian ports, but that question like every other must be considered in connection with its surroundings. I am not so anxiousi to see wheat shipped to Halifax or St. John as to make our farmers in the west pay five cents or ten cents a bushel more to obtain that privilege. I think the true patriotic Canadian spirit is to apply our best energies to the task of so cheapening transportation that we can ship our western products through our Canadian ports at lower rates than, or at least at rates equally as low as those at which they can be shipped through foreign ports. As to this clause I think we are fairly entitled to turn on the hon. gentlemen opposite the arguments they used last year, and instead of using our time and wasting our ability in debating the matter, we can simply say : If hon. gentlemen opposite were sincere last year and really believed that the ultimate advantages, which they predicted would result from the Grand Trunk Railway holding the stock, they shouid leave the original contract as it is and not amend it.
The last clause to which I shall refer is the clause providing for the disposition of the road after the termination of the lease. Although this is dealing with a time fifty years from now, and although they may think what is done then is of little present importance, still it is a grave question In the case of a country which, unlike any individual, is sure to be here fifty years hence. It is a serious question whether we have tin-right to tie up this railway and the adjoining lines of railway fifty years hence, when we do not know what the conditions of the country will be then. Section 11 reads :
In case, during the currency of the lease of the eastern division, the company shall have constructed a branch line or lines running from a point or points in the said eastern division, the government shall, if at the expiration of the said lease, it shall determine to undertake the operation of the said eastern division-
Do what V
-take over such branch line or lines as the company may elect not to retain, at such value as may be agreed upon, or as may, in case of failure so to agree, be determined in the manner provided by paragraph 24 (2) of the said contract, which is hereby made applicable to cases arising under this paragraph.
That is to say, by arbitration. Just see the one-sidedness again ! Where was the junior partner at that time, when the interests of the country were at stake ? Here the Grand Trunk Railway is allowed, through the Grand Trunk Pacific, to operate the road for fifty years, and at the end of that time the partnership is dissolved and the senior partner is allowed to take what he likes, while the junior partner must buy the rest whether he likes it or not Is St not quite conceivable that line after line or utterly unprofitable road may be constructs., built like some recently constructed, lines which have been authorized here for political reasons and for considerations which should not have induced their construction. Yet this unfortunate country, fifty years hence, will have to take them over, because the Grand Trunk will not want them. Why is it in regard to all of these lines, the leased line or .the west line, wherever anything Is to be done at the end of fifty years, the', 'people are ignored and all the rights are given to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ? Surely it is enough to make one feel, as X said before, that Sir Rivers-Wilson well understood with whom he was dealing, when he said it was a partnership between the company and the government of Canada.
And now, I shall -only say _ one word in conclusion. The lion, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton). speaking a day or two ago. wound up his speech very eloquently by explaining the position of the Liberal party. These, Sir, are his closing words :
I have to give my liou. friend (Mr>
R. L. Borden) his answer upon that point, and I have to say that, so far from drawing back, so far from hesitating in connection with this enterprise, this government desires it to be understood that the Liberal party of Canada pledges its political existence on the carrying out of this enterprise.
That is as true as u great many statements that have been made. Is there a gentleman here who does not remember that last session we challenged the lion, gentlemen opposite to stake their political existence, and go to the people who supply the money for the construction of the railway, who will pay the freights upon it and who, of all people, have a right to be heard ? We challenged hon. gentlemen opposite to go before them, we submitted an amendment to the effect that no action should he taken until the people had an opportunity of speaking, and the solid majority voted us down, the contract of which they were so proud, and which was so absolutely final, was passed, but afterwards fell through, and the other party to it comes back with demands even more extraordinary than could have been dreamed of a year ago. Where was the government then, and where was the Liberal party V The Liberal party could not make up its mind for some time whether it would dare to face the people or whether it would creep back to the House. Finally it decided not to face the people and crept back to the House. To-night I again challenge the government to dissolve this House as soon as they see fit; not to pass this iniquitous measure, but to go to the people, who have never given a mandate for the passage of such legislation. The people of Canada were appealed to on a dozen different grounds. In voting they were influenced by free trade or protectionist sentiment, by religious or racial or other reasons. We again ask the government to appeal to the people of this country, who have never given ~ them a mandate to pass such legislation. We challenge them to appeal to the people, and on behalf of the people we say that we are prepared to meet them before the electors, and if the people of Canada decide to pass such legislation, we will humbly bow and assist in the passage of that legislation and in making it as perfect as possible.
